body:
The async convenience methods (`zlib.deflate()`, `zlib.inflate()`, `zlib.gunzip()`, ...) write the input to a Transform and then end it. That's two threadpool round trips per call, one for the data and one for the final flush, plus the stream machinery on top. In a CPU profile of `benchmark/zlib/inflate.js method=inflate`, the main thread sits idle about 71% of the time waiting on the threadpool.

We already have the whole input up front, so this hands it to the handle in a single write with the finish flush, the same way the `*Sync` methods do, and collects the output in the write callback. A call whose output fits in one buffer now takes one round trip. The work still runs on the threadpool.

These stay on the stream path:

- `info: true`, since the engine is handed back to the caller.
- A non-default `flush`, which can change the output bytes.
- `zstdCompress()`. A single `ZSTD_e_end` write makes frames 3–18 bytes larger than `ZSTD_e_continue` followed by `ZSTD_e_end`, so I left it alone.

The output doesn't change. For deflate, gzip, raw deflate and brotli, the old two-write sequence already produced the same bytes as the sync methods. I compared all the async methods plus `gzipSync()`/`deflateSync()` on four inputs (source text, text plus random bytes, a short string, empty) against a build of the base commit: 28/28 outputs are byte-identical, and each build decompresses the other's output.

There are two observable differences. The success callback now runs straight from the write completion, so async_hooks sees it in the `ZLIB` resource instead of a `TickObject`, which is how fs callbacks behave too. `AsyncLocalStorage` context is unchanged, and the new test checks it. Errors still arrive through the `'error'` event like before. Also, `this` inside a non-arrow callback is still the internal engine, but it's never ended now, so `writableEnded`, `writableFinished` and `readableEnded` are `false` (it's still destroyed, with `bytesWritten` set), and `info: true`, the documented way to get the engine, keeps the old stream path.

Two new tests:

- `test-zlib-convenience-async.js` covers the contract: every input type, interop with the sync methods, invalid and truncated input, `maxOutputLength`, `info`, `rejectGarbageAfterEnd`, dictionaries, `finishFlush`, and that the callback never runs synchronously. It passes on the base commit too.
- `test-zlib-convenience-async-round-trip.js` uses async_hooks to check that a small call takes exactly one round trip. It fails on the base commit, which takes two.

### Benchmarks

`benchmark/compare.js`, 40 runs, `n=100000`, against a build of the base commit with the same configure flags. The default `method`/`inputLen` are kept and only `n` is scaled down.

| benchmark | run 1 (loaded machine) | run 2 (quiet machine) | A/A, quiet |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `inflate.js method='inflate'` | +98.11% *** | +94.91% *** ±0.59% | +0.10% |
| `deflate.js method='deflate'` | +62.96% *** | +66.27% *** ±2.34% | +0.34% |

`--max-regression 5` over `deflate.js`, `inflate.js`, `pipe.js` and `creation.js` (20 runs) passes. The sync methods, `createDeflate` writes, pipes and stream creation all stay within about 2%.

Below, Chrome talks to two local servers, one on the base build and one on this PR. It decodes `zlib.gzip()`/`zlib.deflate()`/`zlib.brotliCompress()` responses, and sends `CompressionStream` uploads that the servers decode with `zlib.gunzip()`/`zlib.inflate()`. The payloads match on both, the round trip count drops from 2 to 1, and sequential `zlib.inflate()` calls get faster.
